Content

Five-Year Plans

Pre-Independence

National Planning Committee (1938)

  • It was formed by S.C. Bose.
  • 1st Chairman: J.L. Nehru.
  • It was the first attempt to develop a National Plan for India.

Bombay Plan (1944)

  • "A Plan of Economic Development for India" → popularly known as Bombay Plan. It was prepared by India's leading capitalists like J.R.D Tata.
  • It was published in two parts: First part (released in 1944) and Second part (released in 1945).

Gandhian Plan (1944)

  • The plan emphasized on "decentralised economic structure" for India with "self-contained villages".

Peoples Plan (1945)

  • It was formulated by M.N. Roy, Chairman of the Post-War Reconstruction Committee of Indian Trade Union.

Sarvodaya Plan (1950)

  • It was formulated by Jaiprakash Narayan (formed Congress Socialist Party in 1934). It was a sort of the first blueprint of the planned development of Independent India.

Post-Independence (1947)

  • The concept of five-year plans was borrowed from the USSR (The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) → Joseph Stalin introduced it in 1928 to industrialize the Soviet Union.

Introduction in India

  • The Planning Commission of India was set up in 1950 that prepared the Five-Year Plan.
Pranab Mukherjee served as the Vice Chairman of Planning Commission.

The goals of the five year plans were:

  1. 1. Growth: Growth in terms of GDP.
  2. 2. Modernisation: Integration of new technology in the economy.
  3. 3. Self-reliance: Inward-looking trade strategy (domestic production instead of importing goods).
  4. 4. Equity: Development of all.
  • The Five-Year Plans not only specify the objectives to be attained in the 5 years of a plan but also what is to be achieved over a period of 20 years. This long-term plan is called "perspective plan".

First Five-Year Plan (1st April 1951)

  • Duration: 1951-1956.
  • Based on: Harrod-Domar Model.
  • Key Focus: Agriculture and Rural Development (Primary Sector).
  • It was presented by India's first PM → J L Nehru.
  • Commentary Development Programme (1952) was launched.
  • Target Growth Rate: 2.1%
  • Achieved: 3.6% (Successful)
During Independence, about 75% of the country's population was dependent on agriculture.

Major Irrigation Projects

  • Bhakra Nangal Dam (Sutlej River)
  • 5 IITs were also established.
  • Hirakud Dam (Mahanadi River)
  • Nagarjuna Sagar Dam (Krishna River).

Reforms Introduced in Agriculture

  • Policy of "land of tiller": It was a land reform that gave land ownership to farmers who actually worked on it, instead of landlords. It aimed to end the zamindari system, reduce rural inequality, and empower farmers.
  • Land Ceiling Act (1976): It was a land reform law in India that set a maximum limit on land ownership to prevent concentration of land in the hands of a few and distribute surplus land to landless farmers.
  • High yielding variety (HYV) seeds.

Second Five-Year Plan (Then PM: J L Nehru)

  • Duration: 1956-1961.
  • Based on: P.C. Mahalanobis Model.
  • Key Focus: Development of basic and heavy industries → It stressed more on Rapid industrialisation.
  • The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 (2nd IPR) served as the foundational policy for India's Second Five Year Plan.
  • Three Steel Plants were setup:
  • Rourkela Steel Plant (RSP): Odisha (with German collaboration)
  • Durgapur Steel Plant (DSP): West Bengal (with British collaboration)
  • Bhilai Steel Plant (BSP): Chhattisgarh (with USSR collaboration)
  • Target Growth Rate: 4.5%
  • Achieved: 4.3% (Moderately Successful)
1st steel plant of India: TISCO (Jamshedpur, Jharkhand)

About P.C. Mahalanobis:

  • He is considered as Chief Architect of Indian Planning.
  • On his Birth Anniversary → 29 June, Statistics Day is celebrated.
  • Founded: Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata
  • He started a journal name Sankhya.

Third Five-Year Plan

  • Duration: 1961-1966.
  • Based on: Gadgil Formula.
  • Key Focus: Self-reliant and self-generating economy.
  • Reasons for its failure: Sino-Indian War (1962), followed by the Indo-Pakistan War (1965) → diverted the focus towards defense spending, alongside severe droughts during the plan period.
  • PL 480 Scheme: India imported wheat from the USA under this scheme to alleviate hunger and poverty.
  • Target Growth Rate: 5.6%
  • Achieved: 2.8% (Failure)
Lal Bahadur Shastri was the PM of India during Indo-Pak War. He raised the slogan "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" when India went to war with Pakistan.

Establishment of Various Institutes

  • Food Corporation of India (FCI): 14th January 1965.
  • Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices (CACP): 1st January 1965.
  • Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI): 1st July 1964.
  • Unit Trust of India (UTI): 1963 (by an Act of Parliament) → Established in 1st February 1964.

Plan Holiday

  • A break in Five-Year: 1966-1969 → due to economic strain caused by the war and other factors like severe drought.
  • India focused on "New Agriculture Strategy" or "Green Revolution" → widespread distribution and adoption of HYV seeds.
  • 1st phase (Mid 1960s-1970s)
  • 2nd phase (Mid 1970s)
  • 1971: Bangladesh Liberation War

Fourth Five-Year Plan (Then PM: Indira Gandhi)

  • Duration: 1969-1974.
  • Based on: Gadgil Formula/Rudra-Alien Model.
  • Key Focus: Growth with stability and the move toward self-reliance.
  • Key Initiatives:
  • Family Planning Programme was introduced.
  • 14 major banks were nationalised (1969).
  • First Underground Nuclear Test conducted → "Smiling Buddha" (1974).
  • Drought Prone Area Programme (1973-1974).
  • PM: Indira Gandhi
  • President: V. V. Giri
  • Target Growth Rate: 5.6%
  • Achieved: 3.3% (Failure)

Fifth Five-Year Plan (Then PM: Indira Gandhi)

  • Duration: 1974-1978.
  • Based on: D. P. Dhar Model.
  • Key Focus:
  • Employment and Poverty alleviation ("Garibi Hatao" slogan given by Indira Gandhi).
  • Attainment of self-reliance.
  • Minimum Needs Programme (1974) was introduced which aimed to provide basic needs to poor and unreserved.
  • 20 points programme (1975) was launched that aimed to reduce poverty and improve quality of life.
  • Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were set up (1975).
  • Hill Area Development Programme was initiated.
  • Target Growth Rate: 4.4%
  • Achieved: 4.8% (Moderately successful)

Rolling Plan

  • It was introduced by Janata Party/Morarji Desai government.
  • Duration: 1978-1980.
  • Key Focus:
  • Increase in the country's GDP, employment, and agricultural production.

Sixth Five-Year Plan (Then PM: Indira Gandhi)

  • Duration: 1980-1985.
  • Key Focus:
  • Increase in National Income.
  • Modernisation of technology.
  • Decrease in poverty and unemployment (schemes for transferring skills (TRYSEM → Training Rural Youth for Self-Employment) and seeks (IRDP → Integrated Rural Development Programme) and providing slack season employment (NREP → National Rural Employment Program)).
  • Establishment of NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) in 1982.
  • Rural Landless Labour Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP) was launched on 15 August 1983.
  • Target Growth Rate: 5.2%
  • Achieved: 5.7% (Successful)

Hindu Rate of Growth (1978) → signifying low economic growth

  • Concept given by: Prof. Raj Krishna.
  • From 1960-1980, India has experienced a slow economic growth rate.

Seventh Five-Year Plan (Then PM: Rajiv Gandhi)

  • Duration: 1985-1990.
  • Key Focus (FWP):
  • Accelerating food grain production → Food.
  • Generating employment opportunities → Work.
  • Increasing economic productivity through "Social Justice" → Productivity.
  • Jawahar Rozgar Yojana was introduced in 1989 by merging NREP (National Rural Employment Programme) and RLEGP (Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Programme).
  • Target Growth Rate: 5%
  • Achieved: 6% (Successful)
Department of Biotechnology was set up by GOI in Seventh FYP.

Annual Plans (1990-1992)

  • No Five-Year Plan due to Political Uncertainty.
  • Balance of Payments (BoP) Crisis (1991) that led to beginning of L (Liberalisation), P (Privatisation) and G (Globalisation) reforms.

Eight Five-Year Plan (Then PM: P V Narasimha Rao)

  • Duration: 1992-1997.
  • Key Focus:
  • New Indicative Policy.
  • Economic and Fiscal reforms were seen.
  • Share of Public sector declined (License Raj ended).
  • It focused on Human Development.
  • Target Growth Rate: 5.6%
  • Achieved: 6.8% (Highly successful)
The Eighth FYP could not take off in 1990 due to the fast changing political situation at the Centre and the years 1990-91 and 1991-92 were treated as Annual Plans. The Eighth Plan was finally launched in 1992 after the initiation of structural adjustment policies.
Some 65% of the country's population continued to be employed in agriculture even as late as 1990. Between 1950 and 1990, GDP contributed by agriculture declined significantly but not the population depending on it (67.5% 1950 to 64.9% by 1990).

Ninth Five-Year Plan (Then PM: Atal Bihari Vajpayee)

  • Duration: 1997-2002.
  • Key Focus:
  • Growth with social justice and equality.
  • After 9th Five-Year Plan, there was not much focus on public sector.
  • Target Growth Rate: 6.5%
  • Achieved: 5.4% (Failure)

Tenth Five-Year Plan (by Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Manmohan Singh)

  • Duration: 2002-2007.
  • National Horticulture Mission (NHM) was promoted by government.
  • Jute Technology Mission was introduced.
  • Introduction of Micro Irrigation Programme.
  • Target Growth Rate: 8%
  • Achieved: 7.6% (Failure)

Eleventh Five-Year Plan

  • Duration: 2007-2012.
  • Target Growth Rate: 8%
  • Achieved: 8% (Failure)

Key Focus:

  • Towards rapid and more inclusive growth.
  • Global financial crisis overlapped with the Five-Year Plans.

Twelfth Five-Year Plan (Then PM: Manmohan Singh)

  • Duration: 2012-2017.
  • Key Focus: Towards faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth.
  • Target growth: 8%

NITI AAYOG

  • In 2014, the Planning Commission was replaced with NITI AAYOG and Five-Year Plans were discontinued.
  • NITI AAYOG (non-constitutional body) was set up on: 1st Jan 2015.
  • It is a policy think tank for the GOI.
  • It designs and recommends policies and programs for India's development.
  • It publishes reports on a variety of topics, including fiscal health, education quality, and water management.
NITI AAYOG chairman: Prime Minister of India.

Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR)

  • Industrial Policy Resolutions (IPRs) are policy frameworks set by the Indian government to regulate industrial growth, define the role of the public and private sectors, and promote economic development.

1st IPR, 1948

  • First official industrial policy of independent India.
  • Led by: Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee (Industry & Commerce Minister).
  • It declared the Indian economy as Mixed Economy.
  • Industries were divided industries into 4 categories:
  1. 1. Strategic Industries (Public Sector): Railways, defense, atomic energy.
  2. 2. Basic/Key Industries (Public-Cum-Private Sector): Coal, steel, aircraft, telecommunications.
  3. 3. Industries Requiring Regulation and Control (Controlled Private Sector): Sugar, cement, textiles.
  4. 4. Other Industries (Private and Cooperative Sector): Consumer goods and small-scale industries.
  • The start of License Raj → Government control over industries through licensing.
  • It laid the foundation for public sector dominance in key industries.
In 1955, the Village and Small-Scale Industries Committee, also called the Karve Committee, it noted the possibility of using small-scale industries for promoting rural development.

2nd IPR, 1956

  • It also known as the "Economic Constitution of India".
  • It is a framework for socialist industrial growth in India.
  • Divided industries into three schedules:
  • Schedule A (17 Industries – Public Sector Monopoly) → Aviation, Atomic energy, railways, atomic energy, arms and ammunition, steel and iron, etc.
  • Schedule B (12 Industries – Public & Private Sectors) → Aluminium, machine tools, chemicals, etc.
  • Schedule C (All Other Industries – Private Sector) → Consumer goods, textiles, automobiles, etc.

3rd IPR, 1977 (extension of 1956 Policy)

  • Introduced by Morarji Desai Government (Janata Party).
  • Key Features:
  • It emphasised growth of Small-Scale Industries (SSI).
  • Introduced the "Tiny Unit" concept → Small enterprises with investments below ₹1 lakh.
  • Restrictions on Multinational Corporations (MNCs) → Focus on self-reliance.

4th IPR, 1980

  • It was introduced by Indira Gandhi Government.
  • Key Features:
  • Shifted focus back to heavy industries.
  • Encouraged foreign technology transfer and investment → FERA Act of 1973.
  • Monopolistic and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act, 1969 was amended to remove the threshold limits of assets in respect to MRTP companies.
  • Investment limit for tiny unit increased to ₹2 lakhs.

5th IPR (New Industrial Policy, 1991 → Economic Liberalisation)

  • It was announced by P.V. Narasimha Rao government, led by Dr. Manmohan Singh.
  • Key Features:
  • End of License Raj → Most industries freed from licensing requirements.
  • Privatization → Disinvestment in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs).
  • Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) opened → Allowed foreign investment in key industries.
  • Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization (LPG Reforms) → end of License Raj.

Joint Sector

  • Joint Sector refers to a form of partnership between the public sector (government) and the private sector.
  • Dutta Committee (1973) recommended the establishment of Joint Venture Sector in Indian Industry.

Key concepts

  • Five Year Plans (Harrod-Domar, Mahalanobis, Gadgil Models)
  • Planning Commission and NITI AAYOG
  • Industrial Policy Resolutions (IPR 1948, 1956, 1977, 1980, 1991)
  • LPG Reforms (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation)
  • Green Revolution and Land Reforms
  • P.C. Mahalanobis and P.V. Narasimha Rao
